# Quests TODO — auto-generated `follow_up_quests`

Every quest in this file was drafted by Claude from chapter content as part of
adding the "Tomorrow's Quest" / "Last Night's Story" thread feature. Each item
also carries `auto_generated: true` in the chapter front-matter so it is easy
to find. Review, tweak, or rewrite — and **delete the `auto_generated: true`
flag** (and strike the row here) once you're happy.

The shape per quest is:

```yaml
- kind: sky | ground | story
  text: "..."
  auto_generated: true
```

`kind: sky` is for evening / sky-watching. `kind: ground` is for daylight or
on-the-ground. `kind: story` is for a word, phrase, or hook to carry forward.

---

## `content/chapters/always/moon.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tomorrow night, find the Moon and name its phase aloud. Notice which way the lit side points — that line points straight at the Sun.
- [ ] **ground** — Sometime during daylight, see if you can catch the Moon in a blue sky. First and last quarter are the easiest phases for a daytime sighting.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the word *Tsukuyomi* — the cold Japanese lord of the night — and the small fact that *month* and *Moon* share a root.

## `content/chapters/always/reading-the-sky-by-day.md`

- [ ] **sky** — At dusk, look high up for cirrus 'mare's tails.' If you spot them, predict whether rain arrives in the next 24 hours and check tomorrow.
- [ ] **ground** — Tomorrow morning, do a 30-second cloud census from the breakfast window. Name as many of Luke Howard's ten cloud types as you can see.
- [ ] **story** — Carry Luke Howard's gift — *cumulus, stratus, cirrus* — and try saying *cumulonimbus* aloud the next time a storm builds.

## `content/chapters/winter/orion.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, face south after dusk and find Orion's Belt. Follow the Belt down-left to Sirius and up-right past Aldebaran to the Pleiades.
- [ ] **ground** — By daylight, point south at the patch of sky where Orion will be tonight around 9pm. The hunter is below the horizon, but the bearing is the same.
- [ ] **story** — Carry one Arabic name aloud — *Betelgeuse* (the hand of the Central One) or *Rigel* (the foot). They are some of the oldest sky-words still in use.

## `content/chapters/winter/canis-major-sirius.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, find Orion's Belt and slide down-left to the brightest star in the whole night sky — Sirius. Notice how it twinkles through colours when it sits low.
- [ ] **ground** — Tomorrow morning, work out where due south-east is from your home. That's the rough patch of sky Sirius rises out of on winter evenings.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the Egyptian name *Sopdet* — the morning rise of this one star once warned a civilisation that the Nile was about to flood.

## `content/chapters/winter/taurus-pleiades.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, follow Orion's Belt up-right to the red eye of Taurus (Aldebaran), then keep going to the small fuzzy knot of the Pleiades. How many stars in the knot can you count?
- [ ] **ground** — Tomorrow daytime, ask three people what *Subaru* means — most know it as a car, few as the seven sisters. Show them the badge if you can.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the Māori word *Matariki* — the same little knot of stars, marking the new year in the other hemisphere.

> Note: this chapter is also a stub (`## Draft`). Quests drafted from the
> sources list and the writer's notes inside the file.

## `content/chapters/spring/ursa-major.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, find the Plough. Use Merak and Dubhe as pointers — straight up, five times the gap — and land on Polaris. Check it with a compass tomorrow.
- [ ] **ground** — By daylight, work out which way is due north from your back door. That is where Polaris will sit tonight, no matter the season.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the rhyme *arc to Arcturus, spike to Spica* — and have a go at remembering which Plough-star means *the leader* (it's *Alkaid*).

## `content/chapters/spring/leo.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, face south after dark and look for the Sickle — a backwards question mark high in the sky. The bright dot at the bottom of the hook is Regulus, the lion's heart.
- [ ] **ground** — By day, find the Plough on a star chart and follow the bottom of the bowl down — see for yourself how that line lands on Leo. Then take that geometry outside tonight.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the Arabic *Qalb al-Asad* — *the heart of the lion* — for the bright royal star that sits almost exactly on the Sun's path through the sky.

## `content/chapters/spring/bootes-arcturus.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, find the Plough and trace the arc of its handle outward until you land on Arcturus. Really look at the colour — what name would you give it?
- [ ] **ground** — By day, find Hawai'i on a map. Arcturus passes directly overhead from there — for Polynesian wayfinders it was the latitude marker for the canoe *Hōkūleʻa*.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the Greek *Arktouros* — *guardian of the bear* — and the fact that one star opened the 1933 Chicago World's Fair with a forty-year-old beam of light.

## `content/chapters/summer/summer-triangle.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight after 10pm, lie back and look straight up. Find Vega (brightest), then Deneb to the northeast and Altair to the south. Three stars, one giant triangle.
- [ ] **ground** — Tomorrow afternoon, find a south-facing spot you could lie back in tonight, and check the moon phase. A near-new Moon is your dark-sky window for the Milky Way.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the tale of *Qixi* — Vega the weaver and Altair the cowherd, separated by the river of stars that flows between them, allowed to meet once a year.

## `content/chapters/summer/scorpius-antares.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, find a clear southern horizon and look low for one warm red star — Antares, the heart of the scorpion. From Britain it never climbs high; catch it while summer holds it up.
- [ ] **ground** — By day, scout for a south-facing beach, hill or open field with no trees on the southern horizon. That's your scorpion-watching spot for the next clear night.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the Arabic *Qalb al-ʿAqrab* — *heart of the scorpion* — and the older fact that when Orion rises, this scorpion sets, and they have never met in three thousand years.

## `content/chapters/summer/milky-way.md`

- [ ] **sky** — On the next moonless clear night you can reach a dark-sky site, lie down for thirty minutes with no torch and let your eyes adapt. The pale band that appears is your own galaxy.
- [ ] **ground** — By day, plan the pilgrimage: a dark-sky reserve, a moonless week, blankets, hot drinks, no white light. Put a date on the calendar.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the Greek root: *galaxy* from *gala*, milk. Every galaxy ever named is a sister of one spilled drink.

## `content/chapters/autumn/pegasus-andromeda.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, look high in the south for the Great Square — four stars around a patch of almost-nothing. From Alpheratz, trace the chain northeast to find the faint smudge of the Andromeda Galaxy.
- [ ] **ground** — By day, work out the distance to Andromeda in your own words — 2.5 million light-years, the furthest thing your unaided eye can see. Tell someone the number aloud.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the name *Alpheratz* — one star with two jobs, the navel of the horse and the head of the chained woman. The sky does not mind.

## `content/chapters/autumn/cassiopeia.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, look high in the north for the W of Cassiopeia. Use the deep V of the W to point roughly at Polaris, and check it with a compass.
- [ ] **ground** — By day, work out where due north is from your home. Cassiopeia and the Plough sit on opposite sides of Polaris and take turns being your night-time pointer.
- [ ] **story** — Carry the story of Tycho's 1572 supernova — a new star in this same W, bright enough to see at noon. What would your family do if one appeared tonight?

## `content/chapters/autumn/cygnus-revisited.md`

- [ ] **sky** — Tonight, find Deneb at the top of the Northern Cross. Note exactly where it sits — overhead, high west, low west? Sketch it. Each month it will be lower at the same hour.
- [ ] **ground** — By day, mark on the western horizon you can see from home where Deneb stood last night. The swan dives that way through autumn and is gone from evenings by January.
- [ ] **story** — Carry *Phaethon* — the friend who dove for him became the swan, and the swan flies south each autumn as if still searching.
